content: 1. Tucatinib increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by altering the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Concomitant use of tucatinib with CYP3A substrates should be avoided, as even minimal changes in concentration can lead to severe or life-threatening toxicities. If unavoidable, reduce the dose of the CYP3A substrate as per product labeling and monitor closely. 2. Ethinylestradiol decreases the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 3. Vadadustat increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol through mechanisms not fully understood. Use caution and monitor closely. Vadadustat may also increase the exposure of BCRP substrates. Monitor for adverse effects of BCRP substrates and adjust their dose according to product labeling. 4. Ethinylestradiol and valoctocogene roxaparvovec both increase certain effects (mechanism unspecified). Use caution and monitor closely. Medications that may cause hepatotoxicity when combined with valoctocogene roxaparvovec can increase the risk of elevated liver enzymes. Monitor these medications closely and consider alternatives in case of potential drug interactions. 5. Ethinylestradiol decreases the levels or effects of valproic acid by increasing its elimination, which may lead to increased seizure frequency. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 6. Verapamil increases the levels or effects of etonogestrel by altering the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Voriconazole increases the levels or effects of etonogestrel and ethinylestradiol by affecting the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Zafirlukast increases the levels or effects of etonogestrel by altering the metabolism of the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Reported adverse effects include decreased libido, hypersensitivity reactions (such as anaphylaxis and angioedema), stroke or cerebrovascular accidents, arterial thromboembolic events (including myocardial infarction), and exacerbation of varicose veins. Skin-related issues include urticaria, chloasma, and hereditary or acquired angioedema exacerbations. Reproductive system disorders include penile reactions in male partners of NuvaRing users, galactorrhea, and vaginal injuries associated with ring breakage. 10. Contraindications include documented hypersensitivity, arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), thromboembolic disorders (e.g., DVT/PE), estrogen-dependent neoplasia, cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, severe liver disease, undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding, uncontrolled hypertension, and women over 35 years old who smoke. Avoid use in patients with a history of jaundice related to oral contraceptive use, breast cancer, or estrogen/progestin-sensitive cancers. 11. Use caution in patients with a history of depression, endometriosis, diabetes, hypertension, renal or hepatic impairment, bone metabolic disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus. Conditions exacerbated by fluid retention (e.g., migraines, asthma, epilepsy) should also be monitored closely. 12. Known risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE) include smoking, obesity, and family history of VTE. Discontinue use if arterial or venous thromboembolic events occur or if there is unexplained vision loss, proptosis, diplopia, papilledema, or retinal vascular lesions. Evaluate for retinal vein thrombosis immediately. 13. The risk of VTE is highest during the first year of combined hormonal contraceptive (CHC) use and after restarting CHCs following a break of at least four weeks. The risk gradually disappears after discontinuation. Discontinue CHCs four weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization. 14. Estrogens may cause retinal vascular thrombosis. Discontinue therapy if visual disturbances occur, including migraines, vision loss, diplopia, or proptosis. 15. Women with hypertriglyceridemia or a family history of it may be at increased risk of pancreatitis when using CHCs. Monitor blood pressure in women with well-controlled hypertension and discontinue use if blood pressure rises significantly. 16. CHCs may decrease glucose tolerance. Monitor prediabetic and diabetic women carefully. Consider alternative contraception for women with uncontrolled dyslipidemia, as some may experience adverse lipid changes while on CHCs. 17. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy. Studies also do not suggest teratogenic effects when taken inadvertently during early pregnancy. 18. Oral contraceptives should not be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. If a patient misses two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing oral contraceptive use. 19. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been identified in the milk of nursing mothers, with a few reported adverse effects on the child, including jaundice and breast enlargement. Oral contraceptives may interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative contraception until they have completely weaned their child. 20. NuvaRing is inserted into the vagina and remains in place for three weeks, followed by a one-week break during which withdrawal bleeding usually occurs. A new ring is inserted one week after the previous ring is removed. To maintain contraceptive efficacy, women should adhere to the recommended regimen. 21. Cases of toxic shock syndrome (TSS) have been reported in NuvaRing users. If a patient exhibits signs or symptoms of TSS, consider this diagnosis and initiate appropriate medical evaluation and treatment. 22. Women with liver disease, such as acute viral hepatitis or severe cirrhosis, should not use CHCs. Acute or chronic disturbances of liver function may necessitate discontinuation of CHC use until liver function markers return to normal and CHC causation is excluded. Discontinue use if jaundice develops. 23. CHCs may worsen existing gallbladder disease. Women with a history of CHC-related cholestasis or pregnancy-related cholestasis may be at increased risk for CHC-related cholestasis. 24. The CDC recommends waiting at least four weeks after vaginal birth (if not breastfeeding) or six weeks after cesarean section before initiating CHCs to reduce the risk of VTE. Women with additional VTE risk factors should not use CHCs. 25. The risk of postpartum thromboembolism decreases after the third postpartum week, while the risk of ovulation increases.
